steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a database theory paper on skyline operators for document spanners: motivate extracting only maximal mappings, place it against prior work on spanners and skylines, and lay out our contributions section by section.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The framework of document spanners is an established formalism for expressing declarative information extraction tasks. A spanner specifies the possible ways to assign variables over a textual document. This produces so-called mappings, which are the result of the extraction, and each mapping assigns the variables to a factor of the document, which is called a span. The spanner formalism has been defined using several operators, in particular regular operations extended with capture variables (these correspond to the so-called regular spanners), operators from relational algebra (which can sometimes be translated into regular expressions), string equality (this gives the so-called core spanners), etc.

With the existing operators there is no simple way to extract the mappings that are maximal according to some criteria. But there are natural cases where some mappings are preferred to others. In fact, traditional declarative systems for information extraction have explicit mechanisms to restrict the extracted spans to the maximal ones according to different comparisons. IBM’s SystemT has consolidation rules like “contained-within” (a span dominates its subspans) and “left-to-right” (a span dominates all shorter spans that begin at the same position). The GATE system also has controls such as “Appelt” (which is similar to the “left-to-right” rule of SystemT). Another case is the schemaless context of document spanners, where we can assign spans to only a subset of the variables. There we may want to only capture the spans that assign a maximal subset of the variables and cannot be extended by assigning more variables, in the spirit of for example the relational full disjunction or the OPTIONAL operator of SPARQL.

Fagin et al. proposed a framework to explore the expressive power of operators like controls and consolidators, which enriches document spanners with an earlier concept of prioritized repairs. In it they defined the notion of a “denial preference-generating dependency” (denial pgd), which expresses the binary domination relationship using the underlying spanner language. If this relationship is transitive, applying the denial pgd gives exactly the set of maximal tuples. But they did not look at the computational complexity of this operator, so it has been left open. (Also, their study does not apply to the schemaless context.)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The framework of document spanners is an established formalism for expressing declarative information extraction tasks. A spanner specifies the possible ways to assign variables over a textual document. This produces so-called mappings, which are the result of the extraction, and each mapping assigns the variables to a factor of the document, which is called a span. The spanner formalism has been defined using several operators, in particular regular operations extended with capture variables (these correspond to the so-called regular spanners), operators from relational algebra (which can sometimes be translated into regular expressions), string equality (this gives the so-called core spanners), etc.

With the existing operators there is no simple way to extract the mappings that are maximal according to some criteria. But there are natural cases where some mappings are preferred to others. In fact, traditional declarative systems for information extraction have explicit mechanisms to restrict the extracted spans to the maximal ones according to different comparisons. IBM’s SystemT has consolidation rules like “contained-within” (a span dominates its subspans) and “left-to-right” (a span dominates all shorter spans that begin at the same position). The GATE system also has controls such as “Appelt” (which is similar to the “left-to-right” rule of SystemT). Another case is the schemaless context of document spanners, where we can assign spans to only a subset of the variables. There we may want to only capture the spans that assign a maximal subset of the variables and cannot be extended by assigning more variables, in the spirit of for example the relational full disjunction or the OPTIONAL operator of SPARQL.

Fagin et al. proposed a framework to explore the expressive power of operators like controls and consolidators, which enriches document spanners with an earlier concept of prioritized repairs. In it they defined the notion of a “denial preference-generating dependency” (denial pgd), which expresses the binary domination relationship using the underlying spanner language. If this relationship is transitive, applying the denial pgd gives exactly the set of maximal tuples. But they did not look at the computational complexity of this operator, so it has been left open. (Also, their study does not apply to the schemaless context.)

Maximal matches have been studied a lot in other areas of database research, where this is called the skyline operator. Intuitively, the skyline of a set of results under a partial order relation is the set of results that are maximal, meaning they are not dominated by another result. The complexity of computing skylines has been investigated along many dimensions, for example I/O access, parallel computation, or noisy comparisons. However, we do not know of any study of the complexity of this operator for extracting the maximal matches of document spanners, and this is what the present paper focuses on.

## Contributions.

We present our contributions together with the structure of the paper. After some needed preliminaries (Section 2), we introduce the skyline operator in Section 3. The operator is defined as extracting the maximal mappings of a spanner on a document with respect to a partial order on the mappings, which we call a domination relation. In particular we define the span inclusion, span length, variable inclusion, and left-to-right domination relations, and these cover the examples given above.

To be able to study these operators in a unified way, and similarly to earlier work, we propose a general model where the domination relations are themselves expressed as document spanners. More precisely, a domination rule is a spanner that defines a domination relation on every document: it says which mappings dominate which other mappings, intuitively by capturing pairs (m,m^{\prime}) that indicate that m^{\prime} dominates m. We also focus on what we call variable-wise rules, where the domination relation on mappings can be defined as a product of relations on spans. Put differently, a variable-wise rule is a spanner that expresses which spans dominate which spans, and the domination relation on mappings is obtained pointwise across the variables. This is like the ceteris paribus semantics for preference handling in artificial intelligence or Pareto-optimal points for skyline queries on multidimensional data. All the examples introduced earlier can be expressed in this variable-wise way.

Then we start studying how to evaluate the skyline operator on document spanners, and in Section 4 we begin with the question of expressiveness: does the operator strictly increase the expressive power of spanner formalisms, or can it be rewritten with existing operators? We show that regular spanners are closed under the skyline operator, which generalizes a result of previous work to the schemaless context. On the other hand, we show that core spanners are not closed under skylines, even for the fixed variable inclusion or span inclusion domination relations, which again generalizes a result of that work.

Next we look at whether the skyline operator can be tractably rewritten into regular spanners, so that it can be evaluated efficiently like, e.g., the join operator, which can be compiled in polynomial time in the schema-based context (see Lemma 4.4.7 in an earlier work). In Section 5 we give a lower bound showing that this is not the case: even for variable inclusion domination, applying the skyline operator to a spanner expressed as a sequential variable-set automaton (VA) has a necessary exponential blowup. We show this result by finding a connection between VAs and nondeterministic read-once branching programs (NROBPs). This method is general-purpose and can be used outside of skylines too, and in fact we use it to also show a result of independent interest: there are regex-formulas where the natural join operator has an unavoidable exponential blowup (Theorem 5.5).

In Section 6 we then go from state complexity to the computational complexity of skyline evaluation for regular spanners. This task is clearly tractable in data complexity, meaning for a fixed spanner and domination rule: we just compute all the captured mappings and filter out the ones that are not maximal. More interestingly, if we assume \mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}, we show that the task is intractable in combined complexity, i.e., as a function of the input spanner (Theorem 6.3), and this is already the case for the variable inclusion relation. So we cannot evaluate the skyline operator tractably in combined complexity, even if we do not compile it to an explicit VA.

Finally we study in more detail how the complexity of computing skylines depends on the fixed domination relation: is there any non-trivial domination rule for which skyline computation is tractable in combined complexity? In Section 7 we show a sufficient condition on domination rules, which all the example rules we mentioned satisfy, and which implies (conditional) intractability (Theorem 7.5). Then we show that for a class of domination rules that we call variable-inclusion-like rules, a variant of this condition gives a dichotomy that classifies which of these rules have tractable skyline computation (Theorem 7.7). We end with examples of tractable and intractable rules in the general case.

We conclude in Section 8. Because of space, most proofs are in the Appendix.

Existing operators give no simple way to extract mappings that are maximal according to some criteria. However, there are natural cases where some mappings are preferred to others. In fact, traditional declarative systems for information extraction provide explicit mechanisms to restrict the extracted spans to the maximal ones according to different comparisons. IBM’s SystemT [2] has consolidation rules such as “contained-within” (where a span dominates its subspans) and “left-to-right” (where a span dominates all shorter spans that begin at the same position). Similarly, the GATE system [3] features controls such as “Appelt” (which is similar to SystemT’s “left-to-right”). Alternatively, in the schemaless context of document spanners where spans can be assigned to only a subset of variables [4], we may want to capture only spans which assign a maximal subset of the variables and cannot be extended by assigning more variables, in the spirit of, for instance, the relational full disjunction [5] or the OPTIONAL operator of SPARQL [6].

To explore the expressive power of operators such as controls and consolidators, Fagin et al. [7] proposed a framework that enriches document spanners with the earlier concept of prioritized repairs [8]. There, they defined the notion of a “denial preference-generating dependency” (denial pgd), which expresses the binary domination relationship using the underlying spanner language. When this relationship is transitive, applying the denial pgd yields precisely the set of maximal tuples. However, they did not address the computational complexity of this operator, which has consequently been left open. (Moreover, their study does not apply to the schemaless context.)

The notion of maximal matches has been studied extensively in other areas of database research, where it is called the skyline operator [9]. Intuitively, the skyline of a set of results under a partial order relation is the set of results that are maximal, i.e., not dominated by another result. The complexity of skyline computation has been investigated along many dimensions, e.g., I/O access [10], parallel computation [11], or noisy comparisons [12]. However, we are not aware of any study of the complexity of this operator for extracting the maximal matches of document spanners. This is the focus of the present paper.

## Contributions.

We present our contributions together with the structure of the paper. After some necessary preliminaries (Section 2), we first introduce the skyline operator in Section 3. The operator is defined as extracting the maximal mappings of a spanner on a document with respect to a partial order on the mappings, which we call a domination relation. In particular, we define the span inclusion, span length, variable inclusion, and left-to-right domination relations, which cover the examples presented above.

To allow a unified study of these operators, and similarly to [7], we propose a general model where domination relations are themselves expressed as document spanners. More precisely, a domination rule is a spanner that defines a domination relation on every document: it indicates which mappings dominate which other mappings, intuitively by capturing pairs (m,m^{\prime}) indicating that m^{\prime} dominates m. We also focus on so-called variable-wise rules, where the domination relation on mappings can be defined as a product of relations on spans. In other words, a variable-wise rule is a spanner expressing which spans dominate which spans, and the domination relation on mappings is obtained pointwise across the variables, like the ceteris paribus semantics for preference handling in artificial intelligence [13] or Pareto-optimal points for skyline queries on multidimensional data [12]. All examples introduced earlier can be expressed in this variable-wise way.

We then begin our study of how to evaluate the skyline operator on document spanners, starting in Section 4 with the question of expressiveness: does the operator strictly increase the expressive power of spanner formalisms, or can it be rewritten using existing operators? We show that regular spanners are closed under the skyline operator, generalizing a result of [7] to the schemaless context. By contrast, we show that core spanners are not closed under skylines, even for the fixed variable inclusion or span inclusion domination relations, again generalizing a result of [7].

Next, we ask whether the skyline operator can be tractably rewritten into regular spanners, to allow for efficient evaluation like, e.g., the polynomial-time compilation of the join operator in the schema-based context (see [14], Lemma 4.4.7). In Section 5 we present a lower bound establishing that this is not the case: even for variable inclusion domination, applying the skyline operator to a spanner expressed as a sequential variable-set automaton (VA) incurs a necessary exponential blowup. We show this by identifying a connection between VAs and nondeterministic read-once branching programs (NROBPs). This general-purpose method can be used outside the context of skylines, and we in fact also use it to show a result of independent interest: there are regex-formulas on which the natural join operator incurs an unavoidable exponential blowup (Theorem 5.5).

In Section 6 we then move from state complexity to the computational complexity of skyline evaluation for regular spanners. This task is clearly tractable in data complexity, i.e., for a fixed spanner and domination rule: we simply compute all captured mappings and filter out the non-maximal ones. More interestingly, assuming \mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}, we show that the task is intractable in combined complexity, i.e., as a function of the input spanner (Theorem 6.3), already for the variable inclusion relation. Hence, we cannot tractably evaluate the skyline operator in combined complexity, even without compiling it to an explicit VA.

Lastly, we study in more detail how the complexity of skyline computation depends on the fixed domination relation: are there non-trivial domination rules for which skyline computation is tractable in combined complexity? In Section 7 we show a sufficient condition on domination rules which is satisfied by all the example rules we mentioned and which implies (conditional) intractability (Theorem 7.5). We then show that, for a class of domination rules called variable-inclusion-like rules, a variant of this condition yields a dichotomy classifying which of these rules enjoy tractable skyline computation (Theorem 7.7). We finish with examples of tractable and intractable rules in the general case.

We conclude in Section 8. For reasons of space, most proofs are deferred to the Appendix.
